subject: NetWave: access transport options (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S) - strawman
messages:
From: Ethan Li <ethan.li@netwave.com>
To: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Cc: NetWave NetOps <netops@netwave.com>
Date: 2028-09-15T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private deployment transport - quick context and ask

Kim — thanks for the quick intro earlier. NetWave is evaluating Redwood Private and we need a recommendation for how to connect our on-prem environment (two colo sites + VPCs in us-east-1/us-west-2) to Redwood's private deployment.

High level constraints:
- Regulated PII traffic for a pilot (must not transit public internet).
- Customer wants source IP preserved for internal ACLs and audit trails where possible.
- We have overlapping RFC1918 space in our legacy colo that we can't renumber until Q2 next year.
- Throughput: baseline 200 Mbps, spikes to ~3 Gbps during batch windows.
- Target: low ops overhead for the first 6 months, then tighten for production.

Could you summarize the tradeoffs between (A) VPC Peering, (B) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint, and (C) Site-to-site VPN (IPSec) for our profile, and recommend a primary+fallback approach? Also, any checklist items NetWave NetOps should prepare for the MOP?

Appreciate any strawman — Ethan

--
Ethan Li
Senior Network Engineer, NetWave Systems
From: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Ethan Li <ethan.li@netwave.com>
Cc: NetWave NetOps <netops@netwave.com>, ben_carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-09-15T13:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment transport - quick context and ask

Ethan — thanks for the clear constraints. I sketched a short strawman below (see attached diagram + cost sheet). TL;DR recommendation: start with PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for regulated control-plane/data-plane traffic and a site-to-site VPN as an operational fallback/burst path. VPC Peering can be considered only if NetWave can (a) remove IP overlap and (b) accept cross-account peering limits.

Summary (quick bullets):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints):
  - Pros: strong isolation (Redwood exposes an ENI in your VPC), traffic never traverses the public internet, preserves mutual TLS and per-connection auth at the application layer. Suitable when customers need strict tenant isolation or cannot tolerate DNS/proxy changes.
  - Cons: does not preserve original source IP to your backend (traffic will appear from the endpoint ENI unless we pass X-Forwarded-For at app layer), per-AZ ENI scaling implications (we recommend provisioning endpoints in each AZ you want sub-100ms latency to), potential per-GB data-forwarding charges (we included a line in the spreadsheet). Good if IP overlap exists because PrivateLink avoids route-table changes.
- VPC Peering:
  - Pros: L2-style routing, low latency, source IP preservation (nice for ACLs), and no per-packet interface translation. If both sides are in the same region and you control CIDR space (no overlaps), peering is the lowest-latency option.
  - Cons: not transitive — cross-region or multi-VPC hub patterns require Transit Gateway (adds cost). Requires non-overlapping IPs; with overlap you'd need NAT or readdressing. Management of route tables and security controls is more operationally heavy for cross-account peering.
- Site-to-site IPSec VPN:
  - Pros: easiest short-term to stand up (no cloud account changes), supports active-active with BGP on many appliances, and keeps traffic on encrypted tunnels. Works well to bridge colo to Redwood if you don't want to change VPC topologies.
  - Cons: throughput limits depending on appliance (you mentioned spikes to 3 Gbps — you'd want high-performance appliances or multiple tunnels), potential increased jitter, and added ops to maintain tunnels and BGP. Also, VPNs frequently sit on the public internet (unless you use Direct Connect/Cloud Interconnect + VLAN), so call this a fallback/escape hatch rather than long-term for regulated traffic unless paired with a private interconnect.

Preserving source IP: if preserving original source IP is a hard requirement for application-layer ACLs, VPC Peering (or Transit Gateway with peering) is the only native way to get that without header hacks. PrivateLink will require application-level headers (X-Forwarded-For) or an L4 proxy that rewrites. For auditing we can emit Redwood-level access logs that map client certs to requests if you prefer not to rely on source IP alone.

Suggested primary + fallback (based on your constraints):
1) Primary: PrivateLink for regulated API traffic (interface endpoints in each AZ you need). Why: avoids re-CIDRing, keeps a small blast radius, and simplifies least-privilege exposure.
2) Fallback/Burst: Site-to-site IPSec VPN (or Direct Connect if you have a circuit) for high-volume batch windows and as a resilience path. We can configure a health-based routing policy to failover if endpoint health degrades.
3) Peering: Keep as a later-stage option if you can deconflict IPs and decide to optimize latency/cost once stable.

Operational checklist (short):
- NetWave: confirm which subnets/AZs should host endpoints; provide list of source CIDRs that need access.
- NetWave: inventory of appliances and expected sustained/peak throughput for VPN sizing.
- Redwood: provide IAM role / account numbers and the interface endpoint service names (we'll share after legal/consent).
- Both: test plan for preserving headers and synthetic latency tests; define RTO/RPO for the pilot.
- Security: exchange required CAs and mutual TLS cert details if mutual TLS is required.

Attachments: I attached a small diagram and cost estimate with an example for 1TB/mo egress. Ben/Marissa — looping you for any commercial or compliance caveats.

If you want, we can run a quick 30-min call this week and I can walk the NetOps team through the tradeoffs and the Mutual Action Plan.

Best,
Kim

--
Kimberly Park
Manager, Private Deployments (Redwood Inference)
From: Janelle Ramos <janelle.ramos@netwave.com>
To: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Cc: Ethan Li <ethan.li@netwave.com>, NetWave NetOps <netops@netwave.com>
Date: 2028-09-16T10:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment transport - quick context and ask

Thanks Kim — very helpful. A couple clarifying Qs from NetOps: 
1) You mentioned PrivateLink doesn't preserve source IP. If we rely on X-Forwarded-For, will mutual TLS still authenticate the original client cert? Our auditing team needs cryptographic proof of client identity, not just headers.
2) For the VPN fallback plan: can Redwood automate failover routing from PrivateLink->VPN if an endpoint in an AZ becomes unhealthy? We want the switch to be seamless for our integration tests.

Also, about peaks: we have two colo appliances that can do 3 Gbps each, but public internet latency is variable. We don't currently have Direct Connect in us-west-2. If PrivateLink is primary, are there hidden costs for ’burst reads' when many clients read embeddings?

-Janelle
Network Operations Lead, NetWave
From: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Janelle Ramos <janelle.ramos@netwave.com>
Cc: ben_carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Ethan Li <ethan.li@netwave.com>
Date: 2028-09-18T16:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment transport - quick context and ask

Janelle — good questions. Short answers then concrete next steps: 

1) mTLS + identity proofing: mutual TLS happens at the TLS layer between client and Redwood endpoint. If you require the original client cert for audit, we can terminate mTLS at your PrivateLink ENI and pass a signed assertion (JWT) to Redwood, or alternatively have mutual TLS all the way to Redwood using our network overlay (requires cross-account cert exchange). Practically, most customers combine mTLS + request-level signed tokens so the audit trail is preserved even if source IP is NATed. I'll include a sample flow in the MOP attachment.

2) Failover automation: yes — we can publish an active-health check and a small route automation script on our side. Typical pattern: primary=PrivateLink; route-based probe to endpoint IPs; if probe fails for X seconds, BGP route on your VPN (or policy-based route) is preferred. We'll provide a canonical script and a runbook for toggling DNS TTLs for smoother failover. Note that DNS-based failover has a TTL tradeoff; we prefer route/bgp shifts for sub-minute failover.

3) Burst/egress costs: interface endpoints incur data processing fees (cloud provider dependent) plus our egress estimates. The attached CSV models cost at 0.5TB, 1TB, and 5TB per month including typical reading-heavy embeddings workloads. If you expect sustained multi-GB/s bursts, Direct Connect + private peering to Redwood would be the most predictable economically.

Next steps (mutual action plan - owner assignments):
- NetWave / Ethan: provide subnet/AZ list + confirm which colos will host endpoint routing (due 2028-09-22).
- Redwood / Kim: share interface endpoint service names and our cert CA bundle (2028-09-19).
- NetWave / Janelle: validate VPN appliance throughput and give preferred BGP attributes (2028-09-22).
- Redwood / Ben: draft SLA language for failover behavior and packet-loss thresholds (2028-09-25).

Ben/Marissa — can you take point on the SLA note? Also flag any commercial constraints if PrivateLink egress fees are an issue for the pilot.

I'll schedule a 30-min call for Thursday with NetWave NetOps — can you confirm availability?

Thanks,
Kim
